title: The B12 Blind Spot: A Student's Death Exposes the Hidden Risk in India's Vegetarian Heritage
excerpt: A UK coroner's ruling links a vegan student's suicide to vitamin deficiency — raising urgent questions for millions of Indian vegetarians and a diaspora embracing plant-based living
body:
When Georgina Owen adopted a vegan diet in 2016, she did so for the reasons that motivate millions: compassion for animals, concern for the planet, a desire to live ethically. Five years later, a coroner in Cambridgeshire ruled that the 21-year-old geography student's death by suicide was directly linked to delusional beliefs triggered by severe vitamin B12 deficiency — a deficiency caused by her diet.

The ruling, delivered in May 2026, has sent ripples far beyond Britain. For India's estimated 400 million vegetarians and a growing global diaspora increasingly drawn to plant-based eating, Owen's case is not an indictment of meat-free living. It is a warning about a nutritional blind spot that the subcontinent has quietly endured for decades.

## The Silent Epidemic

Vitamin B12 is essential for producing red blood cells, synthesising DNA, and maintaining a functioning nervous system. It is found almost exclusively in animal products — meat, fish, eggs, and dairy. A deficiency develops slowly, because the body can store the vitamin for years, and its symptoms — fatigue, brain fog, anxiety, difficulty making decisions — mimic stress and depression so closely that they are routinely misattributed.

In Owen's case, three medical experts agreed that her B12 levels had dropped low enough to trigger a progressively worsening psychiatric disorder. Her diaries documented a mind unravelling: fixations on "the state of the world and her place in it," a terrifying out-of-body experience during meditation, mounting anxiety her family could see but not name. She had stopped taking supplements for at least six months, relying instead on an "organic" spray from Canada that likely delivered negligible B12.

India knows this story — not from a single tragic case, but from population-level data that rarely makes headlines. A landmark study from North India found B12 deficiency in 47 per cent of participants. Among vegetarians nationally, research published in PubMed puts deficiency rates between 25 and 86 per cent depending on age group and geography. South Indian vegetarian men face twice the risk of their non-vegetarian counterparts. The British Dietetic Association and India's own ICMR have both flagged the issue, yet routine B12 screening remains uncommon in Indian clinical practice.

## A Tradition With a Nutritional Gap

India's vegetarian tradition is ancient, rooted in Jain ahimsa, Hindu dharma, and regional food cultures that long predate the modern wellness industry. Lacto-vegetarian diets — which include dairy — do provide some B12 through milk, curd, and paneer. But "some" is not always "enough," particularly when dairy consumption is declining among urban, health-conscious Indians, and when the move from vegetarian to fully vegan eliminates the last reliable dietary source of the vitamin.

The trend is accelerating. India's vegan food market, valued at $1.6 billion in 2025, is projected to reach $3.8 billion by 2033, growing at roughly 10 per cent annually. Dairy alternatives already account for 46 per cent of that market. Plant-based restaurants are proliferating in Mumbai, Bengaluru, and Delhi. For NRIs in the United States, Canada, and the UK, the shift is even more pronounced: diaspora communities that grew up in vegetarian households are now gravitating toward veganism, often without the supplementation infrastructure that lacto-vegetarian diets implicitly provided.

## The Philanthropy of Belief

The growing movement is drawing serious institutional investment. Earlier this month, California-based physicians Drs. Jasvant and Meera Modi — Indian American gastroenterologists with roots in Godhra, Gujarat — donated $1 million to establish the first-ever endowed professorship in Vegan and Animal Advocacy Studies at Arihanta Institute, a Jain educational nonprofit. The Tirthankar Shreyansanath Endowment will fund academic research into veganism as an expression of Jain values: compassion, non-violence, and ethical living.

"We are honoured to support this visionary initiative that uplifts two causes very close to our hearts," Dr. Jasvant Modi said. Dr. Modi has previously endowed a professorship in Jain Studies at Rice University. The donation signals something broader: that the Indian diaspora's embrace of veganism is not a passing wellness fad but a philosophical commitment backed by generational wealth and institutional ambition.

## What NRIs Need to Know

The tension is not between veganism and safety — it is between ideology and awareness. Both the British Dietetic Association and the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics affirm that well-planned vegan diets are nutritionally adequate. The operative word is "planned."

For NRIs navigating the shift, the essentials are straightforward but non-negotiable. B12 supplementation — either a daily tablet of at least 250 micrograms or a weekly dose of 2,500 micrograms — is mandatory for anyone avoiding animal products entirely. Fortified plant milks and nutritional yeast help but are rarely sufficient alone. Annual blood tests for B12, folate, and homocysteine levels should be routine, not reactive. Parents raising children on vegan diets face higher stakes: B12 deficiency in pregnancy and infancy can cause irreversible neurological damage.

Following Owen's death, her father helped establish CluB-12, an organisation dedicated to raising awareness about the vitamin and funding research into its neurological effects. The family's message is not anti-vegan — it is pro-vigilance.

For a community whose food traditions have always been inseparable from its spiritual and cultural identity, the lesson is uncomfortable but vital: heritage alone is not a health plan. The richest vegetarian tradition in the world still has a blind spot, and the cost of ignoring it is no longer theoretical.
